questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to try and live in the United States and experience the culture and american way of life. A state I was particularly attracted to was California, due to the many iconic cities such as San Fransisco and Los Angeles as well as its beautiful nature and weather.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Information was fairly accessible, however it is important to read the emails that are sent from the university. Despite them being numerous and many superfluous, some of them do contain very important information and oversight of these could lead to trouble and heartache down the road.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Before arrival we were given the opportunity to be put into small groups with other exchange students. This meant that from the very early stages of the exchange stay you could connect with people, who were in a similar situation as yourself and face the challenges and complications an exchange stay inherently has together. Furthermore, several exchange student events took place at the start of the exchange stay. where socializing was possible. Staff were also - in general - relatively quick and thorough in responding to any questions or problems you had both by email and in person. However, this naturally varied between staff and faculty members.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was hectic and the housing choices available are definitely worse compared to the conditions Danish students are used to. In general students in Isla Vista (the "town" next to the college campus) live many people in one apartment and share rooms either two or three people. This results a more "intimate" and social way of living, which some people will definitely enjoy and others less so. Rent was also more expensive than at home, despite being so many people sharing an apartment or house. The university was - to their credit - very effective at accommodating and prioritising exchange students for campus housing. Myself and other danish exchange students were offered campus housing shortly after applying for it, despite applying very late and there being a long waitlist. I lived on campus for the first 3 weeks until i moved off campus to share an apartment with some other fellow exchange students.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Living off campus gives you more control of your living situation. On campus you are prescribed meal plans and dont have access to any kitchen. It is mostly college freshman who live in the dorms, who on average are around 18-19 years old. Off campus students are typically older, which - all depending on ones own age - may be preferable.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: A month or so prior to the beginning of the quarter you choose your courses. The registration process consists of 3 registration periods. In the first period you can choose two courses and in the second and third period 1 additional course. As an exchange student it is very important to be cleared of any prerequisites a course may have before registration begins. This is done by reaching out to your assigned EAP (Exchange Abroad Program) helper. Unfortunately, course descriptions are very vague and in order to get more information on any given course you have to personally contact professors for the course syllabus, which was a hassle.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The help wasn't the best with respect to course enrollment. You were to some degree left to a type of trial and error process, in which you contacted different university faculty and staff members. This could definitely be improved.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very fortunate and got enrolled in all the classes I wanted. Whether this is luck, my particular major or a general outcome is hard to tell. My impression, however, was that the other exchange students also got most of their chosen courses, but not always - sometimes classes were filled early.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be prerequisite cleared in good time before the first registration pass begins! Use your first registration pass for the subjects that are most important / have highest demand (check prior years).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The academic level was a lot lower and less sophisticated. The econ major had very little math and was a lot less challenging than at home. However, this did vary a lot between courses. Some were very easy courses with no homework and a few multiple choice tests, some unfortunately had more "pseudo" type homework that took time to do, but didn't provide much to any academic improvement. Luckily, others were more challenging and stimulating with well put together homeworks and good curriculum. The easy courses did have the benefit of giving one more time for traveling the country and partake in social activities. The moral of the story is therefore to pick courses wisely and to taper them to your particular wants and desires.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching is a lot more like in a Danish gymnasium. Homework, presentations, tests or quizzes and participation in class during throughout quarter often count toward your final grade.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
-Monetary Economics (ECON 135)
-International Finance (ECON 181)
-Introduction to Game Theory (ECON 171)
-Philosophy of Economics (PHIL 147)
-Introduction to Data Science 1 (CMPSC 5A)
- Financial Market Risk and Modelling (PSTAT 194FM)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: My prefered courses were PSTAT 194FM, CMPSC 5A and ECON 171. These were the courses where I felt I learned something useful and new. The finance course gave a good overview of financial markets as a whole and different types of financial instruments  and the risks involved. The CMPSC 5A was a good introductory course to programming and doing data analysis in Python, where you got quite familiar with the programming language. Finally, Econ 171 was a more challenging and stimulating course with a lot more math, which to me made it quite enjoyable.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Insurance was a huge unexpected cost. I purchased a travel insurance that lived up to the university insurance requirements but I was unable to get it waived. This meant that I had to use their UCSHIP insurance, which cost 15000 DKK and be double insured.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Things unfortunately tended to be more expensive than I was expecting especially food and rent.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: As a part of campus there is a free recreational center available to all students. It has a gym, climbing area, pool as well as tennis, squash, american football and soccer fields/courts. There is also an excursion club administrated by students. As a member you can paddle board, surf and go on weekend trips.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend getting a membership in the excursion club. I would also recommend spending some time in Downtown Santa Barbara. There are plenty of cool and exiting things to do including museum trips, an old franciscan church, whale watching, clubbing and eating out. There are also some cool hot spring and hikes in Montecito.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I would recommend trips to San Fransisco, Los Angeles, Yosemite or/and Sequoia.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was relatively easy, since I understood the language and was accustomed to american culture through movies, news and social media. There were a few ways of greeting people and some slang that may took a short while to get used to, but other than that it wasn't too challenging.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Americans are very friendly and extroverted. They are in general very easy to chat with.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There are very many homeless people in California, who are in very bad condition and often mentally ill. This was quite saddening.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I loved the civil extroversion of Americans. I think we danes can learn from it. I also loved visiting the culturally rich cities of LA and San Fransisco.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Even though an exchange stay may be a daunting idea and your are met with challenges and problems, have faith it all will turn out alright - It usually does :)
2. Be open minded and try new things.
3. Be mindful of appreciating the exchange experience in the present moment - it wont last forever.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Get a bycicle. The walking distances are quite long.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I loved all the traveling and the countless new impressions, experiences and people. As a whole it was an invaluable experience.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: At times missing home, friends and family. However, this wasn't too frequent an occurrence and by no means debilitating in any manor.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Have fun!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
